stem: If the printmaker uses the same amount of ink for every print, how many additional prints, beyond the first 30, can the printmaker pull before exactly 47 milliliters of ink remain in the jar?
stimulus: A printmaker inks a linocut block from a single jar of ink, and every print in the edition uses the same amount of ink. After the 14th print, 262 milliliters of ink remain in the jar. After the 30th print, 182 milliliters remain.
explanation: First, find the rate. Between the 14th and 30th prints, the printmaker pulled 30 − 14 = 16 prints and used 262 − 182 = 80 mL of ink. That is 80 ÷ 16 = 5 mL per print. Start from the 30th print, when 182 mL remain, and let $p$ be the number of additional prints: $182 - 5p = 47$. Then $5p = 135$, so $p = 27$. Reread the question before you answer. It asks for prints beyond the first 30, not the total number of prints, which would be 57.

common_errors.why: Gives the total number of prints (30 + 27) instead of the additional prints after the 30th. You get the same value if you rebuild the starting amount, 332 mL, and solve $332 - 5p = 47$ without subtracting the 30 prints already made.
Starts from 262 mL as if that were the amount after the 30th print: $(262 - 47) \div 5 = 43$.
Stops at the milliliters of ink still to be used, 182 − 47, and doesn't divide by the rate.
Divides all 182 mL by 5 and forgets that 47 mL must stay in the jar.
Gives the ink used per print instead of the number of prints.

stem: How many map sheets will the office print?
stimulus: A county mapping office has a budget of $3,000 for a new set of parcel maps. It pays a one-time licensing fee of $420 for base-map data and buys 6 field tablets at $185 each. It spends the rest of the budget, exactly, on printing large-format map sheets at $15 per sheet.
explanation: Let $s$ be the number of sheets. The whole budget is the fee, plus the tablets, plus the sheets: $420 + 6(185) + 15s = 3000$. The tablets cost $6 \times 185 = 1110$, so $1530 + 15s = 3000$. Then $15s = 1470$, and $s = 98$. Make sure you subtract both the one-time fee and the full cost of all 6 tablets before you divide. Also check that you answer with the number of sheets, not the dollars spent on them.

common_errors.why: Gives the dollars left for printing instead of the number of sheets.
Divides the whole budget by the sheet price and ignores both the fee and the tablets.

stem: If the depth continues to decrease at the same constant rate, on what day will the depth of the reservoir first be 11.4 meters?
stimulus:
A water authority measures the depth of a reservoir during a dry spell. Days are numbered from the start of monitoring, and day 0 is the first day. The depth decreases by the same amount each day.

Reservoir Depth During Dry Spell
Day | Depth (meters)
4 | 18.6
10 | 16.2
explanation: Find the rate from the two readings. The depth falls 18.6 − 16.2 = 2.4 m over 10 − 4 = 6 days, which is 0.4 m per day. Working back to day 0, the depth was $18.6 + 4(0.4) = 20.2$ m. Solve $20.2 - 0.4d = 11.4$: $0.4d = 8.8$, so $d = 22$. You can also start at day 10: $(16.2 - 11.4) \div 0.4 = 12$ more days, and 10 + 12 = 22. The question asks for the day number, not the number of days after the last reading.

common_errors.why: Gives the additional days after day 10 instead of the day number.
Treats the day-4 depth of 18.6 m as the depth on day 0: $(18.6 - 11.4) \div 0.4 = 18$.
Counts the days from the day-4 reading, $(18.6 - 11.4) \div 0.4 = 18$, but then adds 4 to the wrong partial result, or adds 4 to the 12 days counted from day 10. Here: 12 + 4 = 16.
Stops at the day-0 depth found while building the equation.
Gives the daily drop in depth instead of the day.

stem: How many hours after the clinic opens will it run out of doses?
stimulus: A public health department runs a one-day flu vaccination clinic that starts with 1,305 doses. For the first 3 hours after opening, one nurse gives 75 doses per hour. After that, a second nurse joins, and together they give 120 doses per hour until the doses run out.
explanation: Work through the two stages in order. In the first 3 hours the clinic gives $3 \times 75 = 225$ doses, which leaves $1305 - 225 = 1080$. At 120 doses per hour, those last $1080 \div 120 = 9$ more hours. The question asks for the time since opening, so add the first 3 hours: 3 + 9 = 12.

common_errors.why: Gives only the hours at the faster rate and forgets the first 3 hours.
Gives the doses left when the second nurse arrives instead of a time.
Assumes the clinic gives 120 doses per hour the whole day: $1305 \div 120$.
Assumes the clinic gives 75 doses per hour the whole day: $1305 \div 75$.
Subtracts only 75 doses for the first stage instead of 3 × 75: $(1305 - 75) \div 120 + 3 = 13.25$.
